en.title: Robert Downey Jr. Reveals the True Challenge for Avengers: Doomsday
en.summary: The star behind Iron Man, Robert Downey Jr., has reflected on the immense success of Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame. He identifies a significant hurdle that future Avengers installments, potentially featuring Doctor Doom, will face.
en.body:
The sheer scale and emotional weight of **Avengers: Infinity War** and **Avengers: Endgame** set an almost impossibly high bar for future Marvel Cinematic Universe entries. Looking back, **Robert Downey Jr.**, the actor who embodied Tony Stark/Iron Man, understands the unique challenge any subsequent team-up films will face. In a conversation with CBR, he touched upon what made those films resonate so deeply and what that means for what comes next.

**Downey Jr.** pointed to the personal connection audiences forged with the characters and the films themselves. He explained that for many viewers, these movies became markers in their lives, tied to specific memories of where they were, who they were with, and what they were experiencing. This profound, lived-in connection is a powerful force that **Joe Russo**, one of the directors, also acknowledged, describing the intense, obsessive two-and-a-half-year process of crafting **Infinity War** to ensure every hero's arc felt earned and fulfilling for the actors involved.

> "I think people who see the films, they remember where they were at, where they were in school, where they were working, where they were bringing their kid the first time to see one of these films." — **Robert Downey Jr.**

## The Unseen Villain: Audience Expectation
The biggest problem facing a hypothetical **Avengers: Doomsday**, or any future large-scale Avengers narrative, isn't necessarily a charismatic villain like **Thanos** or even a formidable foe like **Doctor Doom**. Instead, it’s the weight of audience expectation and the deep emotional investment built over a decade of storytelling. **Infinity War** and **Endgame** succeeded not just because of their thrilling action or intricate plot, but because they delivered catharsis and closure, albeit through immense sacrifice. They tapped into a collective memory, becoming cultural touchstones. Any new iteration must find a way to recapture that magic without simply rehashing the past, a feat **Downey Jr.** implicitly recognizes.

## A New Era of Stakes
For fans, this means that the anticipated arrival of characters like **Doctor Doom** in a future **Avengers** film will carry immense pressure. It’s not just about introducing a powerful antagonist; it’s about crafting a story that can evoke similar levels of emotional engagement and deliver a narrative payoff that feels both surprising and earned. The success of **Infinity War** and **Endgame** wasn't just about the heroes winning or losing; it was about the journey, the sacrifices, and the shared experience. Future films will need to find new ways to connect with audiences on that fundamental level, ensuring that the *stakes* feel as real and as personal as they did for **Tony Stark** and his fellow Avengers.

What's Next
Details regarding future **Avengers** films, including potential titles, plot points, or villains like **Doctor Doom**, have not yet been announced by Marvel Studios. Fans will need to await official confirmations for any concrete information on upcoming MCU team-up events.

content_raw: In a wide-ranging conversation with CBR about Avengers: Infinity War , star Robert Downey Jr. and co-director Joe Russo have discussed the successful formula behind their Marvel blockbuster and the challenges this year’s Avengers: Doomsday faces as a result. Infinity War shocked fans when it debuted in 2018. It was a high-octane chase movie that ended with the heroes losing and Thanos completing his mission to erase half of all life in the universe. There would be no real happy ending for some of the MCU’s major characters in the follow-up film either, with Downey Jr.’s Tony Stark and Scarlett Johansson’s Natasha Romanoff sacrificing their lives for the cause. Russo acknowledged that Infinity War was tough to pull off, and said he recently confessed to filmmaker Steven Soderbergh that making films like it is “really fucking hard” because they were “grinding it over and over and over obsessively for the two and a half years that we’re working on that project to make sure that [Downey Jr.] is happy and [Chris] Hemsworth’s happy and [Tom] Holland’s happy and [Chris] Evans is happy and Scarlett’s happy and everyone feels fulfilled.” Despite the grind, Downey Jr. cited Infinity War as “the most important” one they’ve done so far, later adding that “I think people who see the films, they remember where they were at, where they were in school, where they were working, where they were bringing their kid the first time to see one of these films.” Looking back at the impact of Infinity War and Avengers: Endgame , Downey Jr. also seemed to understand that Doomsday ’s potential success wouldn’t depend entirely on his performance as the villainous Doctor Doom and that one of the biggest problems facing the film is being compared to the last two Avengers outings. He suggests they’ve found a solution. “It’s not even about how I executed it,” he said. “It’s about the way it’s been structured and the other characters. There’s something going on in Doomsday and forward that is literally the only antidote to ‘How do you not have these films be a letdown after an Infinity War and Endgame ?’ And boy, have we laboured long and hard to bring that.” Russo added, “The stakes keep going up. But emotional complexity is always the answer. You bring emotional complexity to anything, and it enriches it and makes it a fuller experience for the audience. It surprises you. There are a lot of surprises in this, and I think it’s the most emotionally complex of all of them. In a lot of ways, the most mature of all of them.” Marvel Studios has struggled to recapture the highs of Infinity War and Endgame since 2019, spreading itself thin across theatrical releases and Disney+ TV projects.
